blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
The cultural geography of the UK is a senior topic that rewards attention. The four nations — England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland — each carry distinct identities, histories, legal traditions, and even ways of doing business. Within England itself, the North and South differ as profoundly as countries sometimes do: the financial rhythm of the City of London, the industrial directness of Manchester or Leeds, the warmer, more independent spirit of the West Country.

For executives working across the UK, these differences are not decorative. They shape how contracts are negotiated, how employees relate to authority, how customers expect to be treated, and how a product or service needs to be positioned to land well. A campaign that plays in London may fall flat in Glasgow; a tone that works in Belfast may feel wrong in Birmingham.

The senior leader's task is not to memorise every nuance — no one could — but to develop a habit of asking, before any important move, "what does this look like from the other side of the country?" That single question, asked honestly, avoids most of the most expensive mistakes.

items.q: According to the text, why do the UK's regional differences matter to executives?
options: They shape negotiation, authority, customer expectations and positioning
They are largely decorative and best ignored
They only affect marketing campaigns, nothing else
They matter solely in Scotland and Northern Ireland
items.why: "these differences are not decorative. They shape how contracts are negotiated… how a product or service needs to be positioned."

items.q: What is presented as the senior leader's actual task?
options: To relocate operations closer to London
To habitually ask how a decision looks from the other side of the country
To standardise the approach across the whole UK
items.why: "not to memorise every nuance… but to develop a habit of asking… 'what does this look like from the other side of the country?'"

items.q: The example "A campaign that plays in London may fall flat in Glasgow" is used to illustrate that…
options: London campaigns are usually poorly made
campaigns should always be tested first
the same approach can succeed in one place and fail in another
items.why: Inferência: o exemplo mostra que uma mesma abordagem tem recepção diferente conforme a região.

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Regional culture affects how employees relate to authority
Northern directness reflects a real difference in style
Asking an honest question can prevent costly errors
A single UK-wide approach captures every audience equally well
items.why: Inferência: todo o texto argumenta contra a ideia de uniformidade — uma abordagem única perde nuances importantes.

items.q: The phrase "no one could" (about memorising every nuance) suggests that…
options: mastering the detail is impossible, so a good habit of mind matters more
leaders should not try to understand regional culture at all
only locals can lead across the UK
items.why: Inferência: como decorar tudo é impossível, o valor está no hábito de perguntar, não no domínio enciclopédico.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Harry revisando o plano de marketing nacional com o executivo. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, before we sign this off, let me be honest about a couple of things. The deck is strong — but it was built for London, and I don't think you've noticed how London it is. The tone, the pace, the assumption that people will read between the lines. That works brilliantly in the City. It does not travel.

Take Glasgow. Scottish business culture prizes prudence and loyalty — long relationships, careful spending. If we open with the aggressive, move-fast pitch that plays so well here, they'll read it as flashy and a little untrustworthy. We'll lose them in the first two minutes.

And the North of England — Manchester, Leeds — the directness there is not rudeness, it's valued as honesty. They'll respect you far more if you drop the polished hedging and say plainly what the product costs and what it doesn't do.

So I'm not asking you to rewrite everything. I'm asking one thing: for each region, before we launch, look at the plan and ask what it looks like from the other side of the country. Do that honestly and we avoid the expensive mistakes.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What is Harry's main criticism of the deck?
options: It focuses too heavily on Scotland
It is too direct and blunt for any UK audience
It is too short and lacks data
It was built for London without the executive realising how London it is
items.why: "it was built for London, and I don't think you've noticed how London it is."

items.q: According to Harry, what does Scottish business culture prize?
items.why: "Scottish business culture prizes prudence and loyalty — long relationships, careful spending."

items.q: How does Harry say the North of England reads directness?
items.why: "the directness there is not rudeness, it's valued as honesty."

items.q: Why does Harry warn that the London pitch would fail in Glasgow?
options: Because Glasgow audiences dislike all advertising
Because the deck contains factual errors
Because it would be read as flashy and a little untrustworthy
Because the product is too expensive for Scotland
items.why: Inferência: o pitch agressivo choca com o valor escocês da prudência — por isso soa 'flashy and untrustworthy'.

items.q: What is Harry actually asking the executive to do?
options: Check, for each region, how the plan looks from the other side of the country
Cancel the Scottish and Northern launches
Rewrite the entire plan from scratch
Hand the plan over to a local team entirely
items.why: "I'm not asking you to rewrite everything… for each region… ask what it looks like from the other side of the country."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Each nation carries a distinct identity shaped by centuries of its own history." A distinct identity is…
options: a clearly separate and recognisable character
items.why: Distinct identity = identidade distinta: um caráter próprio, claramente diferenciado.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Northern ___ is not rudeness; clients there value plain talk over polished hedging."
items.why: Industrial directness = franqueza industrial, a fala direta valorizada no Norte da Inglaterra.

items.q: "We need to position the service differently for each market." To position something means to…
options: translate it into the local language
present it so it fits how a particular audience sees value
items.why: To position = posicionar: apresentar de forma que faça sentido para um público específico.

items.q: "A friendlier tone helped the campaign land well in Belfast." To land well means to…
options: be received positively by the audience
items.why: To land well = ser bem recebido, cair bem junto ao público.

items.q: "For a senior leader, these regional differences are not merely decorative." Decorative here means…
items.why: Decorative = decorativo: aqui, algo apenas de fachada, sem efeito prático — que o texto nega.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em reuniões sobre planos regionais. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Before we launch, the board still has to sign off on the regional plan." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We'll roll out the campaign region by region, starting in Scotland." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva, por etapas.

items.q: "The Glasgow team pushed back on the aggressive tone of the pitch." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "They agreed to localise the deck but never followed through." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado; aqui, o oposto — não concluíram.

items.q: "Adjusting the tone for the North really helped us build trust with clients." To build trust means to…
options: shorten the sales cycle by force
items.why: Build trust = construir confiança: conquistar credibilidade aos poucos, como diz a lição.
